html:
Makuria was a Christian Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile, in what is now northern Sudan, from about the 6th century to around 1500. Its capital was Dongola, and it is best known for stopping the Arab advance up the Nile in 652.

After the Kingdom of Kush collapsed in the 4th century, three Nubian kingdoms grew up along the river: Nobadia in the north, Makuria in the middle and Alodia in the south. All three became Christian in the 6th century, Nobadia first, through missions from Byzantine Egypt. Early in the 7th century Makuria absorbed Nobadia.

In 652 an Arab army of the Rashidun Caliphate invaded and besieged Dongola. Nubian archers, famous for their aim, beat it back. The two sides then signed the Baqt treaty, a mix of truce and trade deal: Makuria sent enslaved people north each year, and Egypt sent grain, wine and cloth south. It kept a largely peaceful border for some six centuries, a rare case of a Christian state holding off the early caliphates.

The 9th to 11th centuries were its height:

  • Churches and monasteries, including a great cathedral at Dongola, and the painted cathedral of Faras, whose wall paintings survive.
  • Fine painted pottery.
  • Writing in Old Nubian, as well as Greek, Coptic and Arabic.

Makuria's church followed the Coptic patriarch of Alexandria. From the 13th century the Mamluks of Egypt meddled in its succession, Arab nomads moved in, and Muslim rulers took the throne at Dongola. The kingdom faded by about 1500, and the Funj sultanate later took over the region.
